t: LeetCode 1817 - Finding the Users Active Minutes: Deduplicate, Count, Bucket
o: Every log entry is just (user, minute); the same user may appear many times and may even act several times within one minute, but UAM counts distinct minutes only. So user 0 in example 1 acted at minutes 5, 2 and 5 again, which collapses to UAM 2. The output is a histogram: answer[j] is how many users have exactly j distinct minutes, with j ranging over 1..k. In example 1 both users end up with UAM 2, so answer = [0,2,0,0,0]. IDs go up to 10^9, so users must be grouped by a hash map rather than an array indexed by ID; k is guaranteed to be at least every user UAM, so len(minutes)-1 is always a valid index.
k: Per user, only the SET of minutes matters; repeated actions in one minute collapse.
IDs are sparse (up to 10^9), so group with a hash map keyed by ID.
k >= max UAM by constraint, so indexing answer[UAM - 1] is always safe.

a.i: Bucket every action into per-user sets of minutes; the set silently deduplicates repeats. Then each set contributes one count at index size-1 of the answer histogram. This is the natural first idea and runs in linear expected time.
s: Build map user ID -> set of minutes while scanning logs
Allocate answer of size k filled with zeros
a.t: O(n) expected - one pass to insert and one pass over users.
a.sp: O(n) - the map of sets holds every log entry once.

a.i: Sorting the log pairs lexicographically puts all actions of a user together in minute order. One sweep then counts, per user block, how many entries differ from the previous minute - no hash structures needed, trading an O(n log n) sort for lower constant-factor memory overhead.
s: Walk blocks of equal ID, counting minutes that differ from the previous seen minute
At each block boundary add the block UAM to answer[uam - 1]
a.t: O(n log n) - dominated by the sort.
a.sp: O(1) extra beyond sorting in place and the output.

w: Present the hash-map-of-sets version first; mention the sort-and-sweep as the memory-tighter alternative when the interviewer asks about avoiding hashing. Pitfalls: counting duplicate minutes twice, using an array indexed by raw user ID, or writing answer[uam] instead of answer[uam - 1] (the histogram is 1-indexed). Follow-ups: stream-friendly variant (bounded memory needs external grouping), or returning the full per-user UAM list rather than the histogram.
